text: A curb is a limit put on something to hold it back and keep it under control. It does not stop the thing completely, it just fences in how far it can go, which is why you hear about curbs on spending or curbs on pollution. Here the curbs are the rules banning social-media accounts for under-16s.

To flout a rule is to break it openly, without even pretending to follow it. It is stronger than quietly cheating, because part of the point is that everyone can see you doing it. The deck says these bans are flouted, meaning teenagers ignore them in plain sight.

To sidestep something is to avoid it by going around the side instead of meeting it head-on. It comes from the physical move of stepping sideways to dodge a tackle. Rules that are sidestepped are not fought, just quietly got around.

Tactics are the specific moves you try in order to reach a goal. A plan is the big picture; tactics are the individual things you actually do, and you swap them when they stop working. Harini Naidu tried several tactics to cut her son's screen time, one after another.

A restriction is a rule that limits what you are allowed to do. Restricting something means holding it inside those limits, and something restricted has had its freedom cut down. The article uses all three forms about limits on children's internet use.

When a rule is imposed, someone with power puts it in place and everyone else has to live with it, whether they agreed to it or not. Governments impose laws and taxes; a teacher can impose a new seating plan. Australia's ban was imposed in December.

Literally means exactly, word for word, with no exaggeration at all. Many people now use it as a way of saying really, which is the opposite of its strict meaning. When Ms Naidu says the rules literally did nothing, she means nothing changed at all.

Underwhelming means disappointing, because something turned out far smaller or duller than you were promised. It was invented as a joke on the word overwhelming: if overwhelming floods you, underwhelming barely wets your feet. Ishana means the ban made so little difference that people forgot it existed.

A virtual private network, or VPN, sends your internet traffic through another computer somewhere else in the world before it reaches the website. The website then only ever receives that computer's address, not yours, so it responds as though you were in that country. People use them to reach things blocked where they live.

A platform is usually a raised surface, like the one you stand on at a railway station. In technology it means a website or app that other people build things on or post things to, such as YouTube, TikTok or Instagram. Almost every use of the word in this article means a social-media company.

Policymakers are the people whose job is to decide the rules a country follows: ministers, senior officials and lawmakers. A policy is a chosen approach to a problem, so policymakers are the ones choosing it. They are not the people who enforce the rules afterwards.

A lawsuit is a formal complaint brought to a court, where one side claims another side harmed them and asks a judge to do something about it. It is not a crime case with police; it is one party suing another. Families sued Meta claiming its apps harmed young people.

To allege something is to claim it is true before it has been proved. Newspapers and courts use the word carefully, because an allegation is only an accusation so far. The lawsuit alleging harm means that is what was claimed, not what a court decided.

Settling a lawsuit means the two sides agree a deal and end the case before a judge ever rules on who was right. Usually one side pays money or promises changes, and in return the case is dropped. Meta settled by agreeing to change its products for under-18s.

To tout something is to talk it up loudly in public, especially your own success. It carries a hint that the boasting is doing more work than the facts. The Australian government touted early successes before the studies came in.

To write something off is to decide it is a failure and stop counting on it. It comes from accounting, where a business crosses a lost amount off its books. Saying it is too early to write off the rules means it is too soon to call them a flop.

The British Medical Journal is one of the oldest and most respected medical magazines in the world. A journal like this only publishes a study after other scientists have checked the work, which is why news reports treat its findings as solid. Its June study measured whether Australia's ban changed teenagers' habits.

To migrate is to move from one place to another and settle there, the way birds migrate south for winter. People also use it for moving between apps, services or computer systems. The worry was that banned children would migrate to less safe platforms.

Something unfounded is a belief or a worry with no evidence underneath it. The word hides the verb found, meaning to build a base under something, so an unfounded fear has nothing solid holding it up. The fear that children would flood into shadier apps turned out to be mostly unfounded.

The Economist writes large numbers in a shorthand: m stands for million and bn for billion. So 5m accounts means five million accounts. It saves space in a magazine that prints numbers on almost every page.
Aussie is the everyday nickname Australians use for themselves and their country. It is friendly and informal rather than rude. Young Aussies here simply means young Australians.

Keen means eager, really wanting to do something. It is used far more in British and Australian English than American English, where you would more likely say excited or into it. Young Aussies are keen to stay online means they badly want to.

A spy is someone who secretly collects information, but as a verb spy also means simply to catch sight of or notice something. That older sense survives in phrases like spy a chance. When teenagers spy a challenge, they spot one.

A joint is a place where two things meet, like your elbow, and from that comes the other meaning: shared between two or more people. A joint account is one that several people use together. Teenagers share accounts with friends so the age checks cannot tell who is really using them.

To enforce a rule is to make sure it is actually obeyed, by checking on people and punishing those who break it. Writing a rule and enforcing it are two completely different jobs. Much of this article is about rules nobody is really enforcing.

Verification means checking that something claimed is genuinely true. To verify an age, a site has to test the birthday you typed against some kind of proof rather than just believing you. When the testing company opened 50 accounts, only one site did any verification at all.

To beef something up is to make it stronger or tougher, as if adding muscle to it. You can beef up a team, a fence or a set of rules. Australia is beefing up its rules by making the punishments bigger.

To offend usually means to hurt someone's feelings, but in law an offender is someone who has broken a rule. Offending firms are companies caught breaking the law, not rude ones. The fines on them are being doubled.

A$ means Australian dollars, the money used in Australia, which is worth less than an American dollar. So A$99m is ninety-nine million Australian dollars, and the article helpfully adds that this is about 71 million US dollars. Newspapers convert amounts like this so readers everywhere can judge the size.

The eSafety Commissioner is an Australian government official whose whole job is online safety, especially for children. The office can order companies to take material down and can ask them to hand over information. Australia was the first country in the world to create such a post.

A regulator is a government body set up to police one particular industry: writing detailed rules for it, checking that companies follow them, and issuing fines when they do not. Countries have regulators for banks, medicines, airlines and now social media. Malaysia's Communications and Multimedia Commission is its regulator for the internet.

This is the Malaysian government body in charge of the rules for phones, television and the internet in Malaysia. It is the office deciding how the country's under-age social-media ban will actually work. Most countries have an equivalent.

Facial-age estimation is software that guesses a person's age from a photograph of their face. It measures distances and patterns in the image and compares them against millions of photographs whose ages are already known, then outputs its best guess. Because it is only a guess, it often cannot tell a 15-year-old from a 16-year-old.

Age assurance is the general name for any method a website uses to become confident about how old a visitor is. It covers everything from simply asking, to face-scanning software, to demanding a passport. Australia allowed companies to choose their own method; Malaysia is insisting on official identity cards instead.

To distinguish between two things is to tell them apart, to see what makes one different from the other. It is a favourite word of scientists and lawyers because it demands precision. Face-scanning software cannot reliably distinguish a 15-year-old from a 16-year-old.

Victoria is one of Australia's six states, in the south-east of the country, with Melbourne as its capital. Australia is divided into states in much the same way the United States is. Lucina, the 15-year-old whose face was scanned, lives there.
Perth is the main city of Western Australia, on the country's west coast, and one of the most isolated big cities on Earth. Curtin University, where the researcher Tama Leaver works, is based there.

The letters ie are short for a Latin phrase meaning that is. Writers use it to restate something they just said in clearer words. Here it introduces exactly what a real ID means: an official identity card.

A law that is in force is switched on and legally binding right now. Laws can be passed months before they come into force, and they stay in force until they are repealed. Only a few countries have Australian-style restrictions in force so far.

Counsel is an old word for a lawyer, so an organisation's chief legal counsel is its most senior in-house lawyer. That person advises the organisation on what the law lets it do. L.S. Leonard holds that job at Malaysia's internet regulator.

A branch grows off a tree, and the word is reused for any offshoot of a bigger organisation: a bank branch, a shop branch, or a university campus in another country. The University of Nottingham is English but has a Malaysian branch. Tricia Yeoh works at that one.

To comply is to do what a rule requires, so non-compliers are those who fail to do it. You will meet the word constantly in stories about regulation, usually just before a punishment is described. Malaysia says non-compliers may be fined from January.

Being subject to something means being open to it and unable to refuse it. A parcel may be subject to customs checks; a decision may be subject to approval. Here, stored ID cards would be subject to requests from governments, meaning a government could demand to see them.

A suspect is someone the police think may have committed a crime, but as a verb, to suspect something simply means to think it is probably true without proof. Ms Yeoh suspects the platforms are nervous, meaning that is her reading of their behaviour. She is not accusing them of a crime.

A blunt knife has no sharp edge, and a blunt tool cannot do delicate work. Applied to a rule or policy, blunt means crude, hitting everything in its path instead of the exact problem. Critics call outright bans blunt because they sweep up every young user at once.

To get away with something is to do something you should not, and face no consequence for it. Everyone knows the feeling from school. Critics argue that bans let platforms get away with never making their sites safer, because the blame lands on children instead.

To incentivise someone is to give them a reason to do something, usually a reward rather than a threat. The word comes from incentive, meaning a motivating prize. Spelled incentivize in American English, this is the British spelling The Economist uses.

To contemplate something is to think about it seriously and at length, turning it over rather than deciding quickly. Ideas being contemplated are under consideration, not yet agreed. Governments are contemplating ways to push companies into making their sites safer.

Criteria are the standards something must meet before it counts as good enough, like the list of requirements for making a team. One of them on its own is called a criterion. Canada's plan would keep a ban in place until apps meet a set of safety criteria.

To follow suit is to copy what someone else has just done. It comes from card games, where you must play a card of the same suit that was led. The hope is that if one social-media firm adds teen safety limits, its rivals will follow suit.

Credit is money you borrow, but it also means the recognition you get for doing something well. Deserving more credit means deserving to be given more respect for it. Young Australians feel adults do not give them enough credit for handling the internet sensibly.

A filter removes the things you do not want, so something unfiltered arrives raw, with nothing taken out. On a website it means nobody is removing the nasty or false posts. Ms Naidu's son avoids X because he finds it too unfiltered.

A door that has come off its hinges swings loose and uncontrolled, and unhinged describes a person or a place that behaves the same way: wild, unstable, not making sense. It is a common piece of online slang. Calling Reddit less unhinged than X is faint praise for both.
